abstract: Natural movements vary across multiple kinematic features, making it difficult to identify the dynamics shared across movements that generate a behavioral repertoire. Here, we provide a low-dimensional, interpretable generative account of the larval zebrafish hunting repertoire that links tail dynamics to behavioral outcomes. Analysis of thousands of movements spanning classically defined bout types revealed that repertoire diversity arises from continuous combinations of two simultaneously expressed dynamics: a slow, non-oscillatory bending component and a fast, oscillatory undulatory component. An analytical model captured these dynamics with six interpretable parameters and accurately reconstructed movements across the full repertoire and at two developmental stages. Different parameters predicted distinct aspects of movement outcome: maximum tail bend predicted change in heading angle, maximum tail curvature and movement duration predicted distance traveled, and oscillatory asymmetry predicted displacement direction. Relationships among the dynamical parameters constrained the movements and outcomes available to the animal. Key parameters could also be recovered directly from empirical tail kinematics, establishing them as experimentally accessible movement variables rather than model-dependent latent dimensions. Together, these results explain both the diversity and limits of a natural movement repertoire through constrained combinations of co-occurring dynamics.
